utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Good morning to the interpreters, good morning to the Prosecution and the Defence. We are here to resume our case. It is which case, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is case IT-95-14/1-T, the Prosecutor versus Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you. I turn now towards the Office of the Prosecutor. Could we have the appearances, though we know each other very well already.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please, my name is Niemann. I appear with my colleagues, Mr. Meddegoda, Ms. Sutherland and Ms. Erasmus for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: And for the Defence, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. Good morning to our colleagues from the Prosecution. My name is Goran Mikulicic and, together with my colleague, Mr. Joka, I represent the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. As I have said, we are going to resume our hearings, and we shall try to make the best of the time we have this week. Nevertheless, we have slightly changed the timetable for reasons which have to do with the health of Mr. Aleksovski. Therefore, we are going to work from 9 until 1.30, with breaks, so 9 to 10.20, a 20-minute break, and then we shall have another 15-minute break, depending on the circumstances, whether we need to finish with a statement and so on. Therefore, I would like us to make the best of the time and I do not know whether I should take advantage of this opportunity to ask Mr. Mikulicic whether he has any ideas regarding the time required for the presentation of the Defence witnesses. Are you ready to say anything regarding the organisation of work for the Defence, Mr. Mikulicic, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this moment in time, the Defence is not yet quite clear how many witnesses it will call. We roughly estimate that there will be about 20 witnesses, but we cannot be more precise yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will wait for you to be able to give us a more precise indication. I turn now to the Prosecutor, Mr. Niemann. It is up to you, Sir, now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Sir. Your Honours, I just might say at this stage that, as notified in our notice of submission with respect to witnesses, we had originally indicated on the previous sitting that we thought that we would probably complete the Prosecution case this week, but, because of the reduced time, we do not expect that to happen. At the moment we thought the most appropriate witness to take out of the process, because of the time -- that witness we will take will be Professor Biancini and we have done that. It is our expectation at the next sitting we will complete our case, with the conclusion of Professor Biancini's evidence. I thought I should indicate that. I call Daniel Damon, who is our first witness today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: That would be witness 25?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Daniel Damon:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Daniel Damon, can you hear me well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hear you well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You are going to read the solemn declaration that the usher is giving to you, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You may be seated, please. You are now going to answer questions, which the Prosecutor, Mr. Niemann, is going to put to you, please. DANIEL DAMON

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Damon. Would you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am Daniel Damon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And I would ask you, if you would, to cast your mind back to 1992, and at the beginning of the war in the former Yugoslavia. Can you tell us what your occupation was at that stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In fact, before 1992 -- in 1991, I was reporting the war in firstly Slovenia and then Croatia, as a freelance journalist, mostly for Sky News.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps you might tell their Honours, is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sky News is a satellite television service, part of the Murdoch empire.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It operates where, primarily?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is an European service aimed primarily at Britain, but it is visible all over Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What were you covering in particular -- what area of the country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The whole of eastern Europe was my beat, but having begun with the uplifting spectacle of revolution, I ended up my time doing quite a lot of war coverage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And in the early part of 1992, did you have occasion to go into Bosnia and where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I covered the Bosnian conflict from almost the beginning -- the first time I was there was -- apart from travelling through before the war began -- the first time I was there during the conflict was on 25 April 1992. I travelled to Pale by helicopter from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were in Pale, how long did you stay there for approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just for one day at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Then where were you based after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly in Sarajevo until June 1992 -- either in Ilidza in the Hotel Bosna or the Europa Hotel in the centre of town. Because of the situation, I kept -- or we kept, because I was working with my wife at the time, who was a camera operator, we kept a room in both places.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And, during the course of those early days of the conflict, did you have an opportunity to interview some of the leaders of the warring factions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I certainly met many of the leaders -- Dr Karadzic indeed was my first host, if you like, when we flew in by helicopter in 1992, in April. I had some difficulty, because of Sky's logistical problems getting into Sarajevo. In fact, it was with the help of the former Yugoslavian royal family that the helicopter was arranged directly to meet Dr Karadzic. It was intended that we would only stay the one night. I am afraid we cheated and although we did not take any overnight things, we just said, "Sorry we are not getting back on the helicopter", because obviously the whole purpose of our being there was to cover the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, moving on, if I may, to through the course of the year of the war in 1992, I think by Christmas of 1992 you found yourself in Central Bosnia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. By that time, by the late autumn and winter of 1992, we had begun to travel up and down the road from Split quite a lot. We were covering less in Sarajevo by then and more the troubles around Central Bosnia, and we either based ourselves in Kiseljak, or in the town of Vitez -- some of the time we spent staying either close to the British army base, or in a house not far from there, owned by a cafe owner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think one of the places that you visited during this period was Tomislavgrad; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we spent quite a bit of time on Tomislavgrad. It was on the road. It also had its own particular stories. There was a sizeable Serb minority in that area, and obviously that provided some interest, but also it was the logistical base for much of what went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were in Tomislavgrad -- perhaps for the benefit of their Honours, where is Tomislavgrad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is just over the border inside Bosnia from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But it is in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is part of Bosnia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were in Tomislavgrad, did you see troops there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We saw plenty of troops -- not only UN troops but troops of the Croat forces, and it was a base for the Croat forces going in and out of Bosnia, and it was also an important, I think, police point for the Croat authorities, with responsibilities on the border and inside Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say "forces", "Croat forces going in and out of Bosnia", where did those forces emanate from, where did they begin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course this is very difficult for me to say, because we made the assumption -- I say "we" -- all if not -- most if not all journalists made the assumption that the forces inside Bosnia wearing the Croat insignia were from both sides of the Bosnian Croat border. I understand that at this stage it becomes important to be precise and I am not able to be precise, because we were not taking much notice. It seemed to us obvious from both the political background and the logistical background that these troops were -- some of them local Bosnian Croats and some of them Croats from inside Croatia. The only example that I have clearly in my mind of the border crossing is that I did once see a vehicle with the HV plate, as opposed to HVO plate just inside the border on its way to Tomislavgrad. I understand the importance technically of the distinction between troops wearing HV and HVO insignia. We did not take any notice, because for us they were the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you also spent some time with the British battalion there, that was under the command of Colonel Stewart?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Around about 26 October 1992, did you have an opportunity to see troops in training in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We as a team did. Because this was, say, a set-up shooting opportunity -- a set-up filming opportunity -- to see the training, then I sent the crew -- I did not go myself -- to see the training that you are referring to. There were two instances I think which now become more significant than they appeared at the time. One was a parade which took place in Kiseljak of Croat forces, which we filmed -- in fact my wife filmed that, but I was not there, and the second is a quite extensive training with dogs with a kind of paratroop training but out of the back of troops which lots of armies do, and training with guns, which was done in the hills of, I think, Bosnia, above Tomislavgrad. Again, I did not go myself, I sent the crew -- because there was no news dimensions to it in terms of a current story, it was background.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you observe any film that was taken of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw, used and edited those films.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The films that you saw, used and edited, did you make any observations in terms of the preparedness and level of training of these troops?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The troops in the training video were very fit, very well organised, and very well trained, and at that time, because this was before the outbreak of open hostilities between the two Bosnian allies from the Bosnian Government forces and from the several Herceg-Bosna forces, then I must say I was very pleased to see that these Croat forces were very well trained.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: These Croat forces that you saw the films of, they were HVO, were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were wearing HVO insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You mentioned meeting Radovan Karadzic; did you meet any commanders or leaders of particular groups on the Croat side that were working and operating in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At various times, yes. I met Mate Boban, who was the political leader in the southern part of Bosnia in Herceg-Bosna -- I met him in Grude, I met him in Zagreb and I also met him in other parts. I met Tihomir Blaskic in Vitez on several occasions. I met Dario Kordic on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you also meet any paramilitary-type leaders on either side of the conflict at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not meet any of the paramilitary leaders who are the most notorious, no. I met plenty of paramilitaries but not the leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During the time you were covering the conflict did you see any documentation in relation to the conflict that you were able to observe and read?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One particular piece of paper which I was interested in getting hold of and which I did manage to get a photocopy of was dated October 1991 and had various signatures. It was -- as it was described and translated to me -- and you were to remember that my knowledge of the language is only acquired by my being there, I have never learned the language formally so I always needed translation, but I was given a translation of this document, which indicated the setting up of an entity called Herceg-Bosna, and this was a plan from October 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you met Colonel Blaskic that you mentioned a moment ago, what was the nature of the meeting -- what did you discuss with him; what was the object of meeting with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Colonel Blaskic was the man through whom one was able to get permissions to do various things -- to travel to various places or to meet various people. He was a very efficient officer and was very helpful in many ways, when he could be, in arranging passage or in arranging meetings with significant personalities in the Central Bosnia region.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know approximately what area of operation he was involved in at the time -- very approximate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was certainly run from Kiseljak, because in fact the first I heard of him was from another contact in Kiseljak who was one of the senior police officers in Kiseljak who was our first formal contact for making the kind of arrangements I am talking about, and so it ran from Kiseljak, and I think through to Travnik at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In April 1993, did you have an opportunity to see it firsthand -- the conflict that was occurring in and around the Ahmici/Vitez area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. In fact, we had seen the build-up to that in the previous autumn. I remember travelling back to -- my wife was in Zenica and I was in Split. I was travelling back with another cameraman, an Australian, to meet my wife and to bring her back down to the coast, and we were stopped by various barricades and what was called "complications" between the forces wearing Croat insignia, HVO, and those wearing, at the time, TO, which meant the Bosnian Muslim forces, largely Muslim forces, and that was then calmed down. But by April 1993, it had reached a point where there was a clear outbreak of hostilities. When that took place, I was in Tuzla, and, as soon as I heard that the outbreak of hostilities had occurred, particularly in relation to the village of Ahmici, then I immediately set up and it took us about one day to arrive in Ahmici, which we did I think at around 5 o'clock in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you got to Ahmici, what did you see there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We saw the village destroyed. The first obvious example was the minaret of the mosque which was brought down, that was the first thing you could see when you arrived at the village. Then the next thing you saw was the dead animals, because they were lying in the road, and then, as we went up in to the village we saw the bodies of several people -- some of them obviously very young, and some -- well, you could not identify what age or indeed sex they were, but some of them were burned apparently in the doorways of their houses in such a way that they were frozen in attitudes, which, bearing in mind the circumstances, were easy to interpret as horror.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were there, did you see some spent ammunition cartridges or boxes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember one in particular that I think we filmed which had, I would say -- I do not speak any Chinese but I would say had Chinese markings on it. We saw various types of ammunition all over that theatre of course, with lots of different sources -- some apparently from middle eastern countries, some from cyrillic speaking countries, or with cyrillic alphabet and on this occasion from China.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You mentioned a meeting with Dario Kordic. Do you know where he was headquartered or centered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know precisely, because there was a long winding road and quite a difficult process to reach it. Everybody called it "the eagle's nest". We arranged this visit the first time through Colonel Blaskic, with his help, and it was -- we travelled from Vitez up into the hills, that is the best I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And, at a particular meeting with Kordic, when you were, I believe, having dinner, did you discuss with him the question of camps in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was mostly because there were a lot of claims by the Croat side that there were foreign troops, Arab troops, helping the Muslims, as they were described, and so I asked Mr. Kordic to prove this. He was able to do this, after some persuasion, and arranged, a little time later, for us to go to a camp where, indeed, some Islamic prisoners were being held.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did he mention the name of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If he did, then it is confused in my mind with my later understanding of where it was. You have to again remember that most of this was done through translation, and one of the positive aspects of my time there was that we were able, because we had translators who were not from either of the warring factions, but who spoke the language and were trusted as a result, to build up a reasonable relationship between the translators and those major players that we are referring to, so quite a lot of what I achieved was left up to the translators. They knew what we wanted, they carried out the conversations and made the arrangements and, indeed, made quite good relationships at a personal level with some of those involved in the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you say that Dario Kordic had agreed that you could see a camp where these so-called troops or soldiers were. What did you do about that? Can you explain the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went very soon after, maybe not the next day but certainly very soon after, we went to Kaonik and drove up the track towards the camp, which I did not know at the time was a full military camp -- to me, it was just a place with military-looking buildings up in the hills, or up in the hill above Kaonik, above the junction by the bridge, and we, after some negotiation, were taken through to see a building, which looked at first glance to be a store house, and when I went inside I realised it probably was a purpose-built prison, because it had individual cells. There was some difficulty getting that far, but we had the arrangement made, we had proper permission. My recollection is that a phone call was made to confirm that we were who we said we were. I think you can imagine that those soldiers operating the camp did not want western journalists kicking around the place, but, on the other hand, the political leaders could see the advantage in showing some openness to us, so there was a bit of to-ing and fro-ing, persuading those in the camp that we should be allowed to do what we had come to do. We were allowed to see the inside of just one building, and it was, as you say, a prison camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who did you speak to when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the names -- we spoke to, I think -- I have in my mind's eye three officers, three soldiers wearing combats, by which I mean camouflage, one of whom was clearly the senior, but I do not remember any of the faces or the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You say they were wearing camouflage uniforms. Did they have any insignia that you noticed at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were all HVO. At least one of them had the white belt, which indicated the military police, but, again, I do not want to pretend that we went around checking insignias. The distinction, because of the nature of the conflict, for us, between military police and military was very fine indeed. In any of these situations you would often see military police insignia being worn by people who clearly had never had a day's training in their life, so from that point of view any uniform would do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you make a film of the inside of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we filmed the inside of the cells. There were five or six people in each cell. The film that I have since reviewed had five people in one cell. We did not film in another cell -- I went into one other, but, because from a news point of view it was a repetition, we did not bother to film. I just spoke to some of the people in the second cell. I remember one of those more clearly because he was Turkish because he asked me to contact his family and he gave me his name which I wrote down in a notebook which I still have. In the first cell we saw five people. They had no access to water, which seemed to me, because I have travelled in a number of Islamic countries, to be the first obvious pressure on them. Islamic people, if they are religious, which they said they were, need to wash, if at all possible, for their daily prayers and they were very dirty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you able to make any observations about conditions in the prison itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was -- I mean, it was inhuman. I have seen quite a lot of camps and prisons, as you might imagine. This was not the worst, but it was very bad, because there were no facilities, either for access to fresh air or to water, or indeed any sanitary facilities without the involvement of the guards, and, from what I was told by the prisoners, they were not being well treated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And I do not think we have mentioned the date. Do you remember what date it was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know the date because it is written on the tape. Indeed that is always the most accurate record of these things, because bear in mind that is what I am working towards is the finished television product, then the record keeping is best on the television material. It was 14 May 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The tape -- perhaps you might explain to their Honours the tape that we are about to see. The process that you go through that, I think you have a longer running video and then it is made into something suitable for television; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. We film -- I was not operating the camera at the time, there was another camera operator, and he would know that I wanted quite a lot of material, but he would not film continuously, he would film in sections of maybe a minute or more, and then I would take that back to an editing suite and compile it into a report of about a minute and a half, so obviously I would choose from the shots which are there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When your voice appears or is heard on the tape, that is something that you do at the editing suite is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I write a commentary and edit later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On the tape we are about to see it is your voice that one can hear; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please, I now ask that the videotape be played. Mr. Damon, could you explain to us the tape as it is going through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, you have something to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I should like to ask or be told by my learned friend, what is the purpose of seeing this tape? Does the Prosecutor intend to offer the tape into evidence, or is it for information purposes only?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, can you respond, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. This is a tape that we will be tendering into evidence. It is a tape which was contemporaneous with events -- that is 14 May 1993. It is in the period of the indictment. It relates to the camp itself, and, in our submission, on that basis, it is very properly admissible as evidence. This witness was there at the time. There is no feature of hearsay or anything in it that would be objectionable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence had occasion to see this tape, as it was disclosed to us in advance by the Prosecution, so that the Defence is aware of what it contains. The tape includes statements by certain people, who were found there in these premises. We heard from the witness that the tape was edited, that a commentary was added to it later on, that the voice was added on. Since the Defence was not able to address questions or to participate in the compilation of this evidence, the Defence feels that it cannot be admitted, referring to Rule 89(D) and (E), because the Defence was unable to participate on an equal footing in the presentation of this evidence, and that is why we object to its being admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If I may respond to that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This is clearly not a situation where there is any basis whatsoever for objecting to its admission, because the Defence has not had an opportunity to participate in the events at the time. This is a contemporaneous tape, taken at the very time covered by the indictment. On that factor alone it becomes highly probative and it is admissible, because it deals with the subject matter to which this case is entirely concentrating on. If it was made some years later, and the Defence objected to it, there may be some shadow of an objection based on that, but it cannot possibly be objectionable if it is contemporaneous, and that is what it is. The witness has attested to that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, you have something more to add -- have you finished?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I have finished. I just wish to draw attention once again to the fact that the tape is not an integral recording, but it is an edited material. The Defence is not aware of what was left out through the editing process. The Defence might possibly agree with this recording being admitted if at the same time the sound were not to be allowed in, but only the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps I might respond to that, your Honour. There are two versions of the tape given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I am sorry, I was waiting for the interpretation. Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence have been given two versions of the tape. One version, as I understand it, is called "the rushes", which is a technical term used in the industry, which relates to the whole of the taping that takes place -- that has been given to the Defence, as I understand it, unless there has been some breakdown in communication. If that is the case, we would certainly want to correct that. They have been given that, plus the very shorter version. In our submission, your Honour, it does not matter, because of its contemporaneous nature, because it is made at the relevant time, it does not matter whether it is the short version or the long version -- the long version, we have made an assessment that it is not as relevant and in some respects is not relevant at all, and so we have decided not to play that to your Honours. We could do so if the Defence want that to happen, but we do not believe that it would assist you. It is available to the Defence if they see merit in all of that being played -- they are welcome to do so, they have the tape, they can play it in either their own case or in cross-examination if they wish to do so, but, as I say, your Honour, even if those rushes were not available, that is, the longer version was not available, there would still not be, in my respectful submission, any justifiable basis to this objection, because it is contemporaneous with the events in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I am going to consult with my colleagues. (Pause). The Chamber is going to admit this exhibit, this document, in accordance with Article 89(C), because the document was prepared by the witness and the Prosecution did not interfere at all in the process of preparation. We are therefore going to admit the evidence, and the Defence will be able to contest it during the cross-examination, because this document is part of the testimony of this witness. So, you may continue, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours, please. If your Honours just bear with me one moment, I think there has been a confusion on the tapes. (Pause). I understand the matter is now in hand. It will be ready in a couple of seconds, your Honour. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: While we are waiting, I might direct a couple of questions at the witness until the tape is sorted out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Damon, did you interview any of the camp personnel at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not on tape, no. We spoke to them briefly, and one of them, as I think you will see, was willing to close the door with his -- not with his face showing to the camera, but he was there at all times, except that we were able to persuade him to leave us with the prisoners, with the Islamic prisoners for a time. I think he was outside the door but at least it enabled us to talk to them without direct interference.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I believe we might be ready now, so, if we are, would you just look at the tape and perhaps you might -- where this is no commentary, if there are locations relevant, you might mention them as we see them go through the tape. Could the tape now be played? (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We do not have a text. (Videotape stopped)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think there is another segment which follows on slightly after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was the edited version.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is the totality of it. We saw there a very short view of the inside of the prison; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. As I say, we were able to go into two cells, but we only filmed in one. We were not allowed to film outside. That is not unusual, obviously, it was a military position, and we were not allowed, although we did ask to do an on-camera interview with somebody from the Croat guards, but they were not willing to give that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And were the prisoners open with you, do you feel, when you spoke to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as I say we managed to persuade the guard to stand outside. I think that relaxed the prisoners a bit. Also these were quite educated people, and they were determined to have their say. I think they understood that we were who we said we were. I explained to them that I had been to various Islamic countries, so I understood something of their culture. I tried -- it is always the case -- I try to establish some sort of rapport with whoever I am talking to, whatever their background.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the interview that you had with those people that we saw, that interview was on the rushes, as you said -- on another tape?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there is a much longer version of that. You can hear in that longer version that we had quite a lot of detail about how they were kept and, also, the one who was the main speaker in this edited version told me that he had been beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that tape. Might it be given the next number in order.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is exhibit number 75.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, you may now cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Damon, I am Defence counsel representing in this trial the accused, and I shall now address a few questions to you, and please be kind enough to answer them to the best of your recollection. Mr. Damon, could you tell us, please, who did you ask for permission on this occasion to visit Kaonik and to make your recordings there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The visit was arranged with Mr. Dario Kordic at an earlier dinner -- either the previous evening or one evening before that, so the 12th or the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. Mr. Damon, during your period in Central Bosnia, did you have occasion earlier on to meet or to see at any one of the meetings you went to the person named Zlatko Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember meeting the defendant. I know his face, but I cannot distinguish that knowledge from seeing him on the television.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Damon, who was with you in the team when you went to make your photographs in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a translator, a Hungarian from Vojvodina, whose name I would rather not give, he asked me to protect his identity, and there was a cameraman from Zagreb, who holds a Croat passport.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When filming this material, did you record simultaneously the questions and the answers, or did you add on your questions later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The full version contains my questions as recorded at the time, and the answers. What you have seen is a version in fact with none of my questions -- only with my commentary and the answers, but I know that there is in existence the full version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Damon, at the time you moved around quite a bit across Bosnia and we, here, are interested in Central Bosnia. You had contact, I assume, both with military people and with civilians; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that you had contact with local civilians, with the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you remember, can you describe the conditions that prevailed at the time -- I am talking about the first half of 1993 -- in Central Bosnia in the Lasva Valley. When I am thinking of the conditions, I imply supplies of food, electricity, fuel, clothing, footwear and that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The conditions were better than in other parts of Bosnia. There was some cooperation across checkpoints -- although there were by that time distinct, let us say Bosnian and Croat, or Bosnian Croat and Bosnian Muslim areas, which meant that the road from the coast, from where the supplies came, was certainly full of obstacles, but those obstacles did not appear to hold up the flow of food into the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, is it true to say that it was customary to see civilians in that area wearing parts of military uniform, like trousers or blouses -- did you see examples of that during your travels in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no doubt, when somebody was part of a troop or a military formation, yes, you are quite right -- you can see it in London, too -- people wear so-called camouflage either for fashion or because they have nothing better and, indeed, at a time of conflict, people tend to wear that kind of uniform, but there was never any doubt when somebody was acting as part of a military formation, or as a guard on a checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Damon, you said that you went to Tomislavgrad and that you saw many troops there. Could you tell us, what is the road like from Tomislavgrad to Central Bosnia, how long the trip takes and what kind of a road it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, it was largely a dirt road through forest. After the arrival of the British troops, it began to improve, but in that period from, let us say, May 1992 until the following spring, it was a very difficult road to pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that Tomislavgrad, which is very close to the Croat Bosnia border and that you saw there some soldiers with some HV insignias, that is, the Croat army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not say that. I said I saw a truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, that is how I understood you when you said that you saw soldiers from Croatia, so please correct me if I am wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I wanted to make it clear -- what I saw was a truck with HV plates and it had troops in it. I did not see the insignia on the troops. I want to emphasise at the time it seemed to us unimportant, the distinction, because, for example, one of the later commanders of the HVO, Ante Roso, was a former senior officer from the HV, and so that confirmed our acceptance of the situation, which was that HVO troops, brother and sister Croats inside Bosnia, were getting assistance, quite naturally, from Croatia. Whether there were troops crossing or not, I do not offer any evidence, except this one indication, which, to us -- I remember that we noticed it, because it was particularly a Croat army vehicle as opposed to an HVO vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. Could you tell us, Mr. Damon, whether, in the area of Busovaca of Central Bosnia, you ever saw any such examples?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never saw anything like that, that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to your visit to Kaonik. How much time did you spend there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In total, I should say 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You told us that you spoke to these foreign nationals, Arabs, and that you interviewed them -- you asked them certain questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness nods head).

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness nods head).

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We heard from you that one of them, who spoke on behalf of the group, said that they had been beaten; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. I should make clear that they were not all Arabs. One was from Pakistan, another one was from Turkey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you notice on those individuals any marks, any injuries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I saw none, except dirt -- they were very dirty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you ask them who had beaten them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not ask, because it was a collective "they", and it was accepted that we were talking about the guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is that your assumption, or is that your positive knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, you are right, it is an assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that those persons were dirty and that you gained the impression that they had no possibility to use water?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness nods head).

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you ask them anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did. I asked them how they could pray, because I know that Islamic people need to wash, and they demonstrated that their religion allows them to wipe their hands on the wall in order to go through a ritual form of washing, if they are in that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see you have some knowledge about Islamic culture. Are you aware that, during the religious rites, the faithful may also use water from a bottle, if they have no other source of water?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, I am aware, and that is why I asked them how they did it and they demonstrated that they did not have access to any water, but they had to use the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Damon, in the room that you went to, did you see a small cupboard with some things on it, to the right of the door?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the room was completely bare.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I should like to ask the assistance of the usher so that we may show the witness some photographs that have been admitted into evidence as exhibit number 68. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, could the witness put the photographs under the ELMO? Mr. Usher, could you help the witness, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, your Honours, for your suggestion. That was my idea, anyway. Mr. Damon, do you recognise this object that we see on the photograph, on the screen -- do you remember seeing this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have seen this photograph. I understand it was taken during the visit of an European Community Monitor, but I saw this photograph only recently. This object I did not see in the cell, and I was looking for signs of habitation, if you like. It may have been in one of the cells; it was not in the cells which I went into, and I went into two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I should like to ask the usher to show the witness the second photograph, on which we see five persons. (Handed). Mr. Damon, do you recognise these persons on the photograph? Are they the same people that you visited in the cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they appear to me to be the same people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Would you be so kind as to allow us to show the tape once again briefly, if I could ask the technical booth to show us the tape once again, and I thank the usher -- the photographs can be returned to the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Can I ask the audio visual team to show us the tape once again, thank you. (Videotape played) (Videotape stopped)

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can we, for a moment, go back for a moment and play the tape at a slower pace so that we can see the object in the right-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes. Have you understood what Mr. Mikulicic is asking from you? Could you show us the tape, slow motion, so that we can identify the object, which is at the bottom of the picture, the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Lower right-hand corner. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Can you stop for a moment, please -- stop the tape. Is that what you wanted, Mr. Mikulicic? (Videotape stopped)

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can we have the picture on the screen, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: This is the picture you wanted? Can you stop the tape here, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Damon, I draw your attention to the right part of the picture -- it is not clear, because it is dark. When you look at it, could you now identify the object there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see there is a cupboard, but it is not the one in the photograph that you showed me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How can you tell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because what you showed me was a kind of stove and this is much taller, and empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Damon, what I showed you was not a stove; it is an old military cupboard, which used to be used by the former JNA, which was housed in those premises, so, to avoid any misunderstanding, I am not showing you a photograph of a stove?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, I accept what you are telling me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I thank the video department. We can now remove the tape from the screen. Mr. Damon, when commenting on this videotape, you said, and I think I can quote you, "it appears that those people had no occasion to exercise"; is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you explain to us, on the basis of what did you make such a commentary and is this a fact established without any doubt, or is it, again, an assumption?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, this is not an assumption; this is an interpretation -- how can I put it -- this is my way of saying what the prisoners told me, but not reporting it as fact. As journalists we use words like "apparently" and "allegedly" in order to demonstrate that we do not accept what is being told us, but that was something that was told me by the prisoners. I specifically asked them, "Can you exercise?", and they said no. I did not report that as being a statement of fact; I reported it as being "apparent".

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you used the word "apparently", which logically points to an assumption; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it points to a qualification of a reported fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So that is your explanation for the use of those words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What other explanation could there be? I understand that you are trying to ameliorate the conditions which I saw. I am merely reporting the conditions that I saw. They cannot be ameliorated by playing with language.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Damon, perhaps we did not understand one another well. My intention is not to ameliorate any conditions; my intention is to present to the Trial Chamber the facts rather than any conclusions or assumptions. That is my intention. Mr. Damon, were you in a position to bring any things to those people, or to leave them some things that you had with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that was not part of the arrangement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Damon, do you recall whether any one of these persons that you filmed was smoking cigarettes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the cigarette was given by one of the guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Damon, could you tell the Trial Chamber what was the significance of a cigarette at that time in that place, in view of the conditions under which they were obtained at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The significance is that the guards understood that the prisoners were being filmed by a western film crew. It happened on other occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I am not quite sure that you understood my question well. Were you aware of how expensive cigarettes were at the time in Central Bosnia and could one purchase them on the market as one does in London, in The Hague or anywhere else, or in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sure the guards were able to purchase cigarettes. I did not know a soldier who went short of cigarettes throughout the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the situation was with regard to civilians living in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Cigarettes were expensive, but available.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you recall how expensive they were -- I mean, what was the price of the cigarettes, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not smoke, sorry. But cigarettes were the currency and they were expensive, that is true. But the cigarette was given by the guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Damon, after you left Kaonik, did you learn anything about the future fate of the people whom you filmed on your tape, what happened to them in other words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a couple of days later they were exchanged, or at least I assume they were exchanged. We were taken to what was meant to be an exchange or a handover of those prisoners in the centre of Zenica. They were being handed over to the Bosnian Government authorities, with the intervention of an Islamic group or charity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Defence has no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, do you have further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I do wish to re-examine. I notice the time. Perhaps if your Honours wish to take the break now, we can do that after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Niemann. We are going to have a 20-minute break. After that, we will continue with the testimony of Mr. Damon. (10.32am) (A short break) (10.59am)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, you have something to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours. I would like to offer the photograph which was made from the videotape admitted into evidence. I think it may be the number 3 Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, we accept it. You have no objection, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: In that case, Mr. Niemann, you may continue

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This is one of the matters I wish to go to. In the course of the cross-examination just a moment ago by Mr. Mikulicic, Mr. Damon, you were asked a number of questions about observations you made concerning whether or not the men appeared to be beaten. You were asked questions about their sanitary appearance and so forth. I think you were asked questions about the contents of the interview itself. You just heard there was admitted by the Defence an extract of the video that was P75. I would ask you to look at this photograph now, and -- it is in fact clearer -- tell us what it is that you see in the right-hand side of the photograph. (Handed). You should use the exhibit -- that is my copy, I do apologise. Perhaps my copy can be given back to me. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can see what appears to be a cupboard with a cup.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Damon, could you please -- Mr. Usher also -- put the photograph under the ELMO. I think that is better for all of us, so that we can all see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can see a cupboard with what appears to be a cup on top of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. I would ask your Honours now to play the rushes that we did not wish to tender, but seeing as they have now been cross-examined on, I believe that that is now opened the matters up, and in order to resolve any matters of confusion, I seek to play those rushes. It is only a couple of minutes. Mr. Damon, would you look, please, at the television screen, and at the tape that is now to be played?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence has an objection to this method of presentation of evidence by the Prosecution, because, according to the Rules of Procedure, the Prosecution, during the re-examination, after the cross-examination, can only refer to those topics that were raised during the

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: the issue. That is why the Defence objects to the continued questioning by the Prosecution in the sense of seeing additional video tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: One of the golden rules of cross-examination is that if the Prosecution, in their evidence-in-chief, do not present evidence, then if the Defence in cross-examination go into the very issue that is not tendered by the Prosecution, they do so at their peril. They do so at the peril of the Prosecution then leading that evidence. It is a very dangerous course for the Defence to do, but once they do it, this is the consequences of them so doing. Mr. Mikulicic has clearly gone into this second tape. He has done so for whatever reason he thought was appropriate at the time, but now my opportunity arises to not only play that tape so that your Honours can see the tape itself as first evidence, but I will be seeking to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, is that the same tape that we saw during your examination-in-chief and during the cross-examination -- is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour, it is not. It is the other tape that I had mentioned and I said that Mr. Mikulicic had a copy of, but I said that we had refrained from tendering it, because we thought it went broader than was necessary, and for our own reasons did not seek to tender it. When confronted with a situation like that, the Defence have a number of options. If they want to run the risk of the tape being admitted into evidence, they can then start questioning on it. Alternatively, if they want to avoid that, they must very carefully frame their questions so that they do not open up this area. Once it is opened up in cross-examination, then the whole purpose of re-examination is to clarify any of the matters that have arisen in cross-examination. That is clearly what they have done -- they have stepped into this area where they should have otherwise avoided going if they did not want it produced into evidence. Because they have gone into it now, in my respectful submission, the Prosecution should be entitled, subject to your Honours' ruling, to play that tape, to deal with these issues and clarify these issues, and then, indeed, to go the next step and tender it, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: (Pause). The Trial Chamber will not admit the showing of the tape if it was referred to in connection with the conditions shown on the tape that we saw. The Defence touched upon it but only regarding the method of viewing the tape. Therefore, the Trial Chamber will not admit the other tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Mr. Damon, you mentioned that when you were in part of this Kaonik area, you came across individuals who wore camouflage uniforms, either fully, or partly. I was not clear in my mind whether, in your statement, you referred only to people who were members of the paramilitary forces. What I want to ask you is whether you also found civilian individuals dressing in the way you mentioned, as you referred to fashionable people doing so even in London?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I meant to say that there was no doubt, when you met somebody who was part of a military formation, or who was involved at an official level in the conflict -- yes, of course, because many of the soldiers would be living at home, you might see them at another time wearing the trousers, for example, from a camouflage uniform, but the military formations in the area were properly organised, and it was not a rag-tag army in that sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Thank you. My second question relates to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: My second question is meant to be addressed either to Defence counsel or to the accused. I see he has sustained an injury in his right eye. How did it come about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you for asking this question, because the Defence was going to explain at the end of the sitting today that this injury is a consequence of an accident during exercise which he sustained in the detention unit. This is not a consequence of any physical attack or any physical conflict in which my client engaged -- this is accidental injury. I can also state that it has been taken care of, and there is no further need for any medical assistance at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Thank you for your explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO NAVIA
utterances.text: Mr. Damon, I would like to know if you saw an object hanging on the wall of the cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it appears to be a towel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Damon, I also have a few points that I would like to put to you. If I understood well, you said that previously the facilities that you were going to visit appeared to you like a military camp. Afterwards, you realised that it was a prison; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The facility as a whole appeared to be a military camp; the building that we were taken to -- and we were only taken to one -- appeared at first to be a storehouse as part of a military installation. It was not until I got inside that I realised that there were individual cells and therefore it probably was purpose-built as a prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said, I think, if I understood well, that you visited different camps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness nods head).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: And to which party engaged in the conflict did those camps belong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw a camp controlled by the Bosnian army, the Bosnian Government army, in a place called Tarcin and I saw a camp also -- well, not a camp but a prison facility, temporary prison facility controlled by the Bosnian army on the east bank in Mostar, and I saw a camp controlled by the Croat forces in Bosnia in a place called Dretelj near Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: If I understood you well, you also said that the Kaonik camp was not the worst, so if we put it in the affirmative, then one could say that the Kaonik camp was one of the better ones. Why did you say that the Kaonik camp was not the worst?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The worst I saw, because it had so many more people in it and their condition was much worse, was in Dretelj, which was the -- the people were obviously starving and I was taken by some of the prisoners to a -- I think it was an ammunition bunker that they had been kept in, and they showed me some very bad conditions there. These prisoners were not -- did not have the hollow cheeks of the starving. It was their closed confinement, and their insanitary situation which struck me. What you cannot see on the tape is the smell, of course, and it was very unhygienic. So you are quite right, that, in terms of them not being obviously starving, it was one of the better. The prisoners kept in the camp in Tarcin, which was controlled by the Bosnian army, were also hungrier by their appearance than these Islamic prisoners, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: During your testimony, you used, often, words such as "guard", "soldier" and you also said that, at the Kaonik camp, a guard had given the cigarette, but you said at the beginning of your testimony that there were soldiers, but, nevertheless, you did state, I think, that it was possible to make a clear distinction between guards and civilians, so I am asking you two things: there were guards and soldiers; was it possible to make a clear distinction between "guard" and "soldier", as you did between "guard" and "civilian"? I should like to hear your view on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I used the word interchangeably, because they were wearing military uniform. I called them "guard" because they were operating the prison, but they were dressed as soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Then I have no further questions. I think that the Trial Chamber can thank you now for coming to the International Criminal Tribunal, and we wish you a happy journey home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: The next witness, Mr. Niemann, is?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The next witness is witness number 1 in paragraph 2 of our submission in relation to witnesses filed on 20 March 1998. This witness has asked me to make an application for certain measures in relation to the testimony that he will give. He seeks to have the image of his face distorted and to be referred to by use of a pseudonym. We are up to the letter K, pseudonym K at the moment, your Honours. We have advised Mr. Mikulicic of this matter. We have no indication that he is opposed to this application at all, but before I could go into any further detail, it would be necessary to go into private session, unless your Honours are disposed to make the order on the basis of the consent of the Defence. If your Honours are so disposed the blinds could be brought down and the witness brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, do you have anything to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The Defence has no objections to the protective measures as requested by the Prosecution for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. In that case, the measures requested are granted, and we will now go into private session, and I ask the technicians to take the necessary steps for the distortion of the face of the witness, please. (In private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: (In open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Can we continue now? Mr. Niemann, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Witness, the map that is now displayed there, it has certain markings on it. Firstly, before you tell us that, what is the map a map of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The map that you see before you represents the units of the Corps III in the period between December 1992 and January 1993 and portions of the units of the II and the Corps I. The units of the Corps III at that time numbered about 34,000; 10,800 small arms, pieces of small arms, and 80 per cent of the materiel were involved on the front-lines against the Serb and Montenegrin forces; that is Zavidovici, Zepce, Zenica, Travnik, Novi Travnik, Bugojno and Gornji Vakuf. This sector here (indicates) is the sector of Tesanj and Maglaj. At this time the units of army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were part of the Corps II -- part of the Corps III was also involved with those units, and the units that you see over here belonged at this time to the Corps I, and temporarily they were also part of the Corps III, because of the communication lines that existed between the I and the Corps III and we knew that Sarajevo was at that time under a blockade, and, occasionally, some larger forces were engaged in this area. There were three brigades involved in the attempt to deblock Sarajevo. (Indicating on map).

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Just stopping there for a moment, the I, II and Corps III that you have referred to, is the I and II and Corps III of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am talking about the Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: And the locations that are marked on that map and the various Corps -- I, II and III -- that you referred to is relevant for the period December 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I omitted that the blue colour indicates the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; the red lines are the units of the army of the Serb and Montenegrin aggressor and the orange, the HVO units, which, for the most part, were in the settled areas and along the main communication lines. Some minor HVO units were also present in the front-lines against the Serb and Montenegrin aggressor, and they were, together with the units of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, where I point -- this is in the Travnik/Bugojno municipalities, and to the west of Zepce, about 2 kilometres west, but those positions were not marked on this map.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: In order that we might get a better orientation on this map, can you point either to Sarajevo, or the general direction of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sarajevo. (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: So Sarajevo is down in the bottom right-hand corner of the map. Can you point to or the direction of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Banja Luka is to the north-west here. (Indicates). Actually, it is right there. (Indicates). It can be seen on the map.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: It is on the top left-hand corner. Can you point to the city of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here it is. (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: That is approximately the centre of the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, this was a mistake -- here it is. (Indicates). I could not see it properly the first time around.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Can you point to the city of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Busovaca is here. (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Slightly below Vitez. And the city of Zenica, can you point to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zenica is here. (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Now, this map does not show in 1992 the existence of any front -- military front -- between the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. It only shows the front-line at the time of 10 January 1993 until 25 January 1993 in the area of Gornji Vakuf. After that time this front-line was eliminated. In fact, a truce was reached and the trenches were filled in, and the forces were transferred.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: During the course of 1992, and even up to the time that that map is depicted, what role did the HVO play in the conflict, particularly with respect to the conflict between the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Serb/Montenegrin forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the beginning the units of the Croat Defence Council and the Croat population, which was also threatened by the Serb and Montenegrin aggressor, we decided to jointly resist the Serb/Montenegrin aggressor.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Now, was this done by the HVO dividing up the specific parts of the front with the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or did they work in cooperation with each other, or was it a little bit of both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the most part, we held portions of the front-lines in a combined way, depending on what was rational. Where the population was Croat, it was held by the HVO units, and where the Bosnian population prevailed, it was manned by the BiH army and later it was by agreement -- even though the HVO units were better equipped, they had a third of the personnel in their units, but they had much better equipment and better weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Now, in the early part of 1993, did this arrangement of holding the front with the HVO -- did this arrangement come apart?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it came apart. In fact, in certain parts of the front, the units of the Serb and Montenegrin aggressor and the HVO units starting openly cooperating and there were some attacks against the populated areas and at that time mostly the members of the Bosnian army units were either killed, arrested, or driven out and this was especially the case in the area of Zepce in early 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: How did the HVO conduct the war against the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1993 -- how did they go about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The BiH army units at the end of 1992 and early 1993 were organised by three offensives in order to effect a deblockade of Sarajevo and this was from the direction of Zenica in the direction of Sarajevo. During this period of time, while the BiH army units were engaged there, the HVO authorities tried to take over control in certain towns of Central Bosnia, so the Bosniak population and units were attacked in Vitez, Novi Travnik, Travnik, Busovaca and Gornji Vakuf, with the goal of taking over the local authorities, the municipality, the police, and establishing the authority of the Croat Defence Council there.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Did this happen at any particular time or according to any pattern, these attacks that took place, that you were able to observe when you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was happening to us and I gave you an example on 28 December 1992 -- this was at a moment when it was an attempt to deblockade Sarajevo, that was the most organised, and at that time the HVO attacked right at that same time in this area of Central Bosnia which I just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: So, in other words, did you gain the impression that, when the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was at its most committed in relation to a particular plan of attack, that it was at that time that HVO attacks took place -- would that be a fair assessment of what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: I think you have prepared another map, have you, of the central area of Central Bosnia, in particular the area of Vitez, Busovaca and Zenica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: And again it was prepared on a similar basis to the map that you have now displayed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: I think you would seek to take back the original of those maps with you, but you have no difficulty with them being fully copied and copies being kept here and copies made available for the Defence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I agree to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I now tender this map. If it may be tendered on that arrangement so that it can be uplifted and the original sent back to Sarajevo. We have put that in train. I seek to tender that map as the next exhibit in order.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is Exhibit 77.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Witness, would you just tell us what that is a map of, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a map -- this is for the deployment of forces for the operative area of Lasva in April 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: And it is a more detailed map of the Lasva Valley area than the one we have just previously seen, Exhibit 77?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is the deployment of forces of the HVO units and the BiH army units.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: All the markings that appear on that map were placed on there by you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be advised to speak into the microphone?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The interpreters are having difficulty hearing you. I know it is a bit awkward, but could you lean forward and speak more into the microphone, because they cannot hear your voice. Thank you. Now what I would like to do, witness, is to have that part of the map that relates to the Busovaca Vitez area displayed on the ELMO machine and I would ask you some more detailed questions about that specific area, if I may. Again, witness, when you point to the map, please point to it on the ELMO machine and not on the television screen in front of you. In addition to that, would you please sit yourself in such a way that you can speak into the microphone and point to the map at the same time. If the ELMO machine could be activated by the technicians, please. Just take your time. Looking at that map, I wonder if you would firstly point to the River Lasva, where it flows, please, down from Vitez. Just show us the line of the map where that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Lasva River flows in this direction, and here it flows into Bosnia, which then flows towards the north. This is the Lasva River, and it flows into the Bosna River. (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Can you point to the city of Zenica, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zenica is here. (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: The witness is pointing on the screen to the top right-hand side. Can you point to the city of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: And the town or city of Busovaca, if you could point to that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Immediately north of Busovaca, can you see if you can locate on the Lasva River the place known as Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Now, we have certain markings that you have placed on that map. Firstly, the red or orange coloured markings broken line, which appears to go around Kaonik, can you tell me what the red or orange line represents that you have marked there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The red circles indicate the deployment of the HVO forces.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: What about the broken line that you see there, what does that indicate -- the broken line that runs right across the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This broken line means that they were halted in their attack, in their offensive.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Who is "they"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Is that the HVO lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I said units of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Now, what does the blue broken line represent?
